raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure secondary to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction near the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, when no alternative cause is identified [1–4]. Modern definitions generally require reduced LV ejection fraction (LVEF), usually <45%, and emphasize that PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion, not simply “heart failure in pregnancy” [3–7]. Because dyspnea, fatigue, edema, and orthopnea overlap with normal late pregnancy and puerperium, delayed recognition remains common and clinically important [5,7,29].

Epidemiology varies strikingly by geography and ancestry. U.S. administrative and population-based studies estimate PPCM in roughly 1 per 800–4,000 deliveries, with rising coded incidence over time and disproportionate burden among Black women [8–10]. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, advanced maternal age, multiparity, and multiple gestation are repeatedly associated with PPCM [8–12]. These associations likely reflect both shared biology—especially anti-angiogenic signaling—and social determinants influencing access to timely diagnosis and specialist care [10–12,29].

Pathophysiology is multifactorial. Early work described inflammatory activation and elevated cytokines in affected women [15]. A major mechanistic advance came from experimental models in which cardiomyocyte STAT3 deficiency increased oxidative stress and cathepsin-D-mediated cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa anti-angiogenic fragment, producing endothelial injury and cardiomyopathy [16]. A complementary vascular model showed that late pregnancy creates an anti-angiogenic milieu, including soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), which can provoke PPCM in susceptible hearts [17,21]. MicroRNA-146a has been implicated as a mediator of prolactin-fragment toxicity and a candidate biomarker [18]. Genetics further modifies susceptibility: truncating variants in dilated-cardiomyopathy genes, particularly TTN, occur in a meaningful minority of PPCM patients and overlap with familial dilated cardiomyopathy [19,20,25].

Diagnosis begins with clinical suspicion and urgent echocardiography. Findings include reduced LVEF, LV dilation of variable degree, functional mitral or tricuspid regurgitation, right ventricular dysfunction, and intracardiac thrombus in severe cases [4,5,7]. Natriuretic peptides are helpful because they are not usually markedly elevated in normal pregnancy; electrocardiography, chest imaging, troponin, renal and liver function, thyroid testing, and evaluation for pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, myocarditis, valvular disease, sepsis, and congenital or pre-existing cardiomyopathy are guided by presentation [4,5,22]. Cardiac magnetic resonance can clarify alternative diagnoses and tissue characterization, but acute management should not wait for it when heart failure is evident [5,22].

Management depends on pregnancy status and severity. Stable postpartum patients are treated with guideline-directed therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, including diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin system inhibition, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and contemporary heart-failure agents when compatible with lactation and local guidance [4,5,23,24]. During pregnancy, fetal safety restricts therapy: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided; hydralazine–nitrate combinations, selected beta-blockers, loop diuretics, and anticoagulation when indicated are commonly used [4,22–24]. Severe acute PPCM requires a multidisciplinary pregnancy heart team, intensive monitoring, early delivery planning if antepartum and unstable, vasodilators or inotropes as appropriate, and early consideration of temporary mechanical circulatory support as a bridge to recovery [22].

Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin, is the principal disease-specific therapy studied. A small randomized proof-of-concept trial suggested improved LVEF and clinical outcomes with bromocriptine added to standard therapy in severe acute PPCM [26]. A later multicentre randomized study compared short and longer bromocriptine regimens in postpartum PPCM and supported feasibility and substantial recovery, although definitive placebo-controlled mortality data remain limited [27]. Meta-analytic data suggest improved LVEF and recovery with prolactin inhibition, but evidence remains heterogeneous; bromocriptine should be paired with anticoagulation because of thrombotic concerns and individualized against breastfeeding goals [24,27,28].

Prognosis is variable but often favorable with early treatment. In the North American IPAC cohort, most recovery occurred within 6–12 months; lower baseline LVEF, larger LV size, Black race, and delayed diagnosis predicted worse recovery [13,14,29]. Persistent LV dysfunction, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, need for LV assist device or transplantation, and death occur in a clinically important minority [12–14,22]. Decisions about wearable or implantable defibrillators should account for the potential for reverse remodeling; permanent devices are usually deferred unless dysfunction persists after optimized therapy [14,22].

Long-term care includes serial echocardiography, optimization and cautious duration of heart-failure therapy after apparent recovery, contraception counseling, psychosocial support, and genetic counseling/testing when family history, severe disease, or cardiomyopathy-gene variants are suspected [20,24,25]. Subsequent pregnancy is highest risk when LVEF has not normalized, but relapse can occur even after recovery; shared decision-making should include maternal risk, fetal risk, surveillance plans, and alternatives to pregnancy [24,30].
